idiom_name: DB-API 2.0 cursor + fetchall()/description (sqlite3.Row for named access)
implementation_notes: PEP 249 makes the row set a stdlib object: cursor.execute() produces a cursor, cursor.fetchall() returns the remaining rows as a list, and cursor.description is the column header (7-item tuples whose first element is the column name; sqlite3 fills the rest with None). What replaces the classic RecordSet class is the cursor's materialised list plus its description; with connection.row_factory = sqlite3.Row each row is sequence- and mapping-like, so a cell is readable by index (row[0]) or name (row["email"]). The classic hand-written structure is still justified when header and rows must travel as one value - a small dataclass (columns: list[str], rows: list[tuple]) is then the pattern in Python form.
code_sketch:
con = sqlite3.connect("app.db")
con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
cur = con.execute("SELECT id, email FROM customer WHERE active = 1")
rows = cur.fetchall()                       # materialised, detached rows
cols = [d[0] for d in cur.description]      # column header
print(cols, rows[0]["email"], rows[0][0])
pitfalls: fetchall() materialises every row - use fetchmany()/iteration for large results; also note that cursor lifetime rules differ per driver (sqlite3 keeps cursors usable after commit, PostgreSQL drivers invalidate them).
Without a row factory, rows are plain tuples: positional access breaks silently when the SELECT list changes; sqlite3.Row or dictionary rows restore name access.
Driver-specific cell types (Decimal, datetime, memoryview for blobs) make the set non-JSON-serialisable and non-portable; convert at the boundary.

variants.name: pandas DataFrame (columnar record set)
variants.idiom_name: pandas.read_sql_query / DataFrame with columns and dtypes
variants.implementation_notes: pandas is the dominant data-shaped record set in the Python stack: read_sql_query() materialises a query result into a DataFrame that carries the column header plus per-column dtypes, supports vectorised filtering/projection, and converts back to plain rows with to_dict('records'). What replaces the classic structure is the DataFrame itself - choose it when the consumer is analytical (column operations, joins, group-by) and the DB-API row list when the consumer merely forwards rows. The column header is stronger than PEP 249's description (types, not just names), but every cell lives in a numpy array, so string-heavy or mixed-type results cost more memory than a row list.
variants.code_sketch:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_sql_query("SELECT id, email FROM customer WHERE active = 1", con)
df.dtypes                       # column header + inferred types travel with the value
df.loc[df["email"].str.endswith("@acme.com"), "id"].tolist()
pitfalls: dtypes are inferred per column from the SQL result; object columns hold Python objects (NaN for NULL), so 'typed' is weaker than it looks.
Wide VARCHAR-heavy results are boxed into object arrays: memory and CPU costs can dwarf the equivalent DB-API row list.
